name: Anniversary
seoDesc: Anniversary: work out anniversary name from the anniversary date and the time of getting married. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the anniversary date and the time of getting married and the Anniversary calculator solves for anniversary name. It suits a practical question that turns up in daily life. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Anniversary calculator work?
sections.html:
The Anniversary calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports anniversary name in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select your anniversary year); then you give the anniversary date and the time of getting married.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A calendar date. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I remember the time I got married!”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A time of day. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 100 options, such as 1st, 2nd and 3rd. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A date and a time of day. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Anniversary calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

You've been together for=calculate age on − time of getting married − anniversary date
Your next anniversary is in=(anniversary date, time of getting married, calculate age on)
Days differenceerence=(anniversary date)
Hours differenceerence=(anniversary date, calculate age on)
Minutes differenceerence=(anniversary date, calculate age on)
Seconds differenceerence=(anniversary date, calculate age on)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in years / months / days
  • Time, opening in days / hours / minutes

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Anniversary calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the anniversary date and the time of getting married — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Anniversary calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns anniversary name, derived from the anniversary date and the time of getting married. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Anniversary calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the anniversary date and the time of getting married, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter you've been together for in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. You've been together for opens in years / months / days and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports You've been together for = -0.003 hrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Anniversary calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
